title: A/An and The: Introducing and Identifying Nouns
summary: Choose a/an when introducing or classifying a singular countable person or thing, and the when the listener can identify which one is meant. Use shared context, descriptive details and common frequency expressions to make the choice.
learningObjectives: Introduce an unfamiliar singular countable noun with a/an and refer back to it with the.
Choose the for objects or people identified by surrounding context or a specifying phrase.
Distinguish a person’s profession or an unknown example from a particular known person or place.
Use a/an in rates and frequency expressions such as once a week and twice a day.

explanation.heading: Introduce with a/an and refer back with the
explanation.body: Use a/an when mentioning a singular countable person or object without assuming that the listener knows which one. On a later mention, the can identify that same item. This is not simply about first versus second position in a paragraph: what matters is whether the listener can identify the intended referent.
explanation.example: I found a bracelet on the path. The bracelet had a small silver charm.

explanation.heading: The points to a particular identifiable person or thing
explanation.body: Use the when both speaker and listener can tell which person or object is intended. A phrase such as beside the printer or that you recommended may make the reference specific. A/an, by contrast, can mean one unspecified member of a class.
explanation.example: Please hand me the folder beside the monitor.

explanation.heading: Shared situations can identify a noun without earlier mention
explanation.body: Sometimes the context makes a thing obvious even when nobody has named it before. In a meeting room, the projector may be the one everyone sees; at a café, the manager may be the person responsible for that business. Common destination expressions include the bank, the post office, the doctor and the dentist when the context supplies a recognisable role or place.
explanation.example: Could you lower the blinds? The afternoon sun is on the screen.

explanation.heading: A type of person versus an identified one
explanation.body: When stating somebody’s profession or classifying an unknown member of a group, use a/an with a singular countable noun: my cousin is a surveyor. Use the for a particular person or thing that is already understood: the surveyor who inspected this bridge. Whether the noun sounds familiar to the speaker is not enough; consider what the listener can identify.
explanation.example: We need an electrician, but the electrician we usually call is on holiday.

explanation.heading: A/an also expresses frequency and rates
explanation.body: Use a/an in expressions that mean each or per, including once a month, four days a week, twice a day and forty pounds an hour. These are established ways to describe regular frequency, working hours or unit prices. The is not normally interchangeable with a/an in these rate expressions.
explanation.example: The shuttle runs three times a day during the festival.

left.label: Introducing a noun
left.example: I spotted a kite above the sports field.
left.note: A kite introduces one not-yet-identified object.

right.label: Referring back
right.example: The kite landed beside the fence.
right.note: The kite refers to the object that has just been introduced.

comparisons.title: An occupation versus a particular practitioner

left.label: A member of a profession
left.note: A classifies Yasmin by her occupation.

right.label: A specific appointment
right.example: I have an appointment with the dentist tomorrow.
right.note: The dentist refers to the practitioner understood from the appointment context.

examples.sentence: A guest left a blue backpack at reception.
examples.note: A guest and a blue backpack introduce new, unspecified individuals or objects.

examples.sentence: The backpack is now behind the reception desk.
examples.note: The backpack refers to the object introduced earlier in the conversation.

examples.sentence: Please switch off the fan above the door.
examples.note: The specifying phrase above the door identifies which fan is meant.

examples.sentence: My neighbour is an interpreter who works at conferences.
examples.note: An describes a profession without identifying a particular known interpreter.

examples.sentence: This gym offers guided sessions twice a week.
examples.note: A week means per week in a frequency expression.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I saw a suitcase by the lift. A suitcase was bright yellow.
commonMistakes.correct: I saw a suitcase by the lift. The suitcase was bright yellow.
commonMistakes.why: The second sentence refers to the same suitcase already introduced, so use the.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Please turn off a projector by the window.
commonMistakes.correct: Please turn off the projector by the window.
commonMistakes.why: When the window phrase identifies the intended projector, use the.
If the sentence introduces Nora’s occupation rather than a known specific position, use a.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The exercise class meets twice the week.
commonMistakes.correct: The exercise class meets twice a week.
commonMistakes.why: Twice a week is the normal frequency expression; a means per.

studyTips: When choosing an article, ask whether your listener could identify one particular person or thing from the conversation or situation.
Tell a short two-sentence story about one object: introduce it with a/an, then use the for the same object.
Memorise complete rate expressions such as once a day, three times a month and sixty kilometres an hour.

exercises.prompt: At the market I bought a pear. Later, ___ pear turned out to be ripe.
exercises.feedback: A introduces the pear, and the identifies that same pear when it is mentioned again.

exercises.prompt: Could you switch off ___ lamp beside your chair? It is too bright.
exercises.feedback: The phrase beside your chair identifies which lamp the speaker means.

exercises.prompt: My sister is ___ dentist, but she has the day off today.
exercises.feedback: A describes her profession rather than one particular dentist known to the listener.

exercises.prompt: The evening class meets twice ___ week.
exercises.feedback: Twice a week means two times per week, so use a.

exercises.prompt: On Sunday I found ___ (old key) under the steps. Write the indefinite article and adjective + noun.
acceptedAnswers: an old key
exercises.feedback: Old starts with a vowel sound, and the key is newly introduced.

exercises.prompt: At the park I spotted a bicycle by the gate. Later, ___ (bicycle) had disappeared. Use the definite article and noun.
acceptedAnswers: the bicycle
exercises.feedback: The identifies the same bicycle that was mentioned in the previous sentence.

exercises.prompt: The meeting room is hot. Please open ___ (window beside you). Write the definite article and the given noun phrase.
acceptedAnswers: the window beside you
exercises.feedback: The phrase beside you identifies the intended window.

exercises.prompt: The bus leaves three times ___ (day). Write the article and singular noun.
acceptedAnswers: a day
exercises.feedback: Three times a day is a regular frequency expression.

exercises.prompt: The same wallet is meant in both sentences. Correct only the article in the second sentence: We found a wallet. A wallet was empty.
acceptedAnswers: We found a wallet. The wallet was empty.
exercises.feedback: The second reference is to an already introduced wallet, so the is appropriate.

exercises.prompt: There is one projector by the window and both speakers know which one. Correct only the article: Please switch off a projector by the window.
acceptedAnswers: Please switch off the projector by the window.
exercises.feedback: The identifies the particular projector in the shared setting.

exercises.prompt: The sentence states a profession, not a known position. Correct only the article: The new colleague is the architect.
acceptedAnswers: The new colleague is an architect.
exercises.feedback: An architect classifies the colleague by occupation; the is not warranted for an unspecified member of the profession.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the article in this rate expression: The printer produces twenty pages the minute.
acceptedAnswers: The printer produces twenty pages a minute.
exercises.feedback: A minute means per minute in a rate expression.

speakingExercises.prompt: Tell a friend about a purchase using exactly two sentences. Given facts: I / buy / scarf / yesterday; it / be / blue. Use “a scarf” in the first sentence and “the scarf” in the second. Begin with “I bought”.
acceptedAnswers: I bought a scarf yesterday. The scarf was blue.
speakingExercises.feedback: The first sentence uses a for a new item; the second uses the for the same scarf.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe a new sighting in one sentence. Use these words in order: I / saw / an unusual bird / in the garden. Start with “I saw”.
acceptedAnswers: I saw an unusual bird in the garden.
speakingExercises.feedback: An introduces a previously unidentified bird and precedes the vowel sound in unusual.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask someone politely to close a particular window. Begin “Please close” and finish “the window beside the desk”.
acceptedAnswers: Please close the window beside the desk.
speakingExercises.feedback: The identifying phrase tells the listener which window to close.

speakingExercises.prompt: State Mila’s profession in one complete sentence using the exact words: Mila / be / dentist. Begin “Mila is”.
acceptedAnswers: Mila is a dentist.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use a when identifying someone’s occupation.

speakingExercises.prompt: You need any suitable bank nearby, not one already selected. Ask one complete question beginning “Is there” and ending “near here”, using “a bank”.
acceptedAnswers: Is there a bank near here?
speakingExercises.feedback: A bank means any suitable bank, not a particular one both speakers have identified.

speakingExercises.prompt: You mean the particular bank on Pine Street. State one plan. Begin “I need to go to” and finish “the bank on Pine Street”.
acceptedAnswers: I need to go to the bank on Pine Street.
speakingExercises.feedback: The street phrase makes the intended bank identifiable.

speakingExercises.prompt: Report this fixed frequency in one complete sentence: the artist / work / six days a week. Begin “The artist”.
acceptedAnswers: The artist works six days a week.
speakingExercises.feedback: A week is the normal per-week frequency expression.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences using these facts, in order: there / be / a printer / in the office. The printer / be / new. Use the article a on the first mention and the on the second.
acceptedAnswers: There is a printer in the office. The printer is new.
There's a printer in the office. The printer is new.
speakingExercises.feedback: A printer introduces it; the printer identifies the same device already mentioned.

listeningExercises.audioText: This morning I bought a travel mug. The mug keeps my tea hot for hours.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which item keeps the speaker’s tea hot?
choices: A thermos owned by a friend.
listeningExercises.feedback: The mug refers back to the travel mug introduced earlier.

listeningExercises.audioText: Could you lower the blinds by the door? The sunlight is reflecting off the screen.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker ask someone to adjust?
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker identifies the blinds by their position near the door.

listeningExercises.audioText: Zoe works as a translator for an international charity.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word occupation phrase immediately after “as”.
acceptedAnswers: a translator
listeningExercises.feedback: A translator is the spoken phrase identifying Zoe’s profession.

listeningExercises.audioText: I need a mechanic to check the brakes, but I don't know anyone in this town.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker indicate about the mechanic?
choices: A familiar mechanic has already agreed to help.
The mechanic has finished the repair.
The speaker has not identified a particular mechanic.
listeningExercises.feedback: A mechanic indicates any suitable person in the profession, not a known individual.

listeningExercises.audioText: I know the receptionist at this hotel, but I've never met the manager.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which person has the speaker not met?
listeningExercises.feedback: The manager identifies the person in that role at the hotel, and the speaker has not met them.

listeningExercises.audioText: The swimming pool offers lessons twice a day, once in the morning and once in the evening.
listeningExercises.feedback: Twice a day identifies two daily sessions, reinforced by morning and evening.

listeningExercises.audioText: Please give me the folder on the top shelf.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word noun phrase immediately after “me”.
acceptedAnswers: the folder
listeningExercises.feedback: The folder is the definite noun phrase heard after me; the shelf phrase identifies it.

listeningExercises.audioText: The taxi service charges fifteen pounds an hour for waiting time.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word rate expression immediately after “pounds”.
acceptedAnswers: an hour
listeningExercises.feedback: An hour means per hour, and hour starts with a vowel sound.
